Medicine 08.question: ১) What type of pathogen causes gonorrhoea?
Medicine 08.exp:
Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae (a Gram-negative diplococcus). It primarily infects the genital tract, but may also affect the rectum, pharynx, and conjunctiva.

The other options:

  • Virus: Causes infections such as HIV, herpes, and hepatitis B, but not gonorrhoea.

  • Fungus: Causes infections like candidiasis.

  • Parasite: Causes diseases such as trichomoniasis (caused by Trichomonas vaginalis).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gonorrhoea → Neisseria gonorrhoeae

  • Type → Gram-negative intracellular diplococcus

  • Spread → Sexual transmission

  • Common symptom → Purulent urethral discharge

Exam Pearl:
Gonorrhoea is caused by a bacterium: Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Medicine 08.question: ২) Which is a pathognomonic lesion of scabies?
Medicine 08.exp:
The pathognomonic lesion of scabies is a burrow. It is a thin, wavy, thread-like track in the skin created by the female Sarcoptes scabiei mite as it tunnels into the stratum corneum to lay eggs.

The other options:

  • Papule: Common in scabies due to hypersensitivity reaction but not pathognomonic.

  • Crust: Seen in severe scabies (e.g., crusted scabies) but not diagnostic.

  • Comedone: A feature of acne vulgaris, not scabies.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Scabies organism → Sarcoptes scabiei

  • Pathognomonic sign → Burrow

  • Common sites:

    • Finger webs

    • Wrist

    • Genital area

    • Axilla

  • Intense itching, especially night-time pruritus

Exam Pearl:
Burrow = Pathognomonic lesion of scabies.

Medicine 08.question: ৩) tinea capitis involves.....?
Medicine 08.exp:
Tinea capitis is a dermatophyte fungal infection of the scalp and hair shafts. It is most common in children and may present with:

  • Scaly patches on the scalp

  • Hair breakage

  • Patchy hair loss (alopecia)

The other options:

  • Trunk: Involved in tinea corporis (ringworm of the body).

  • Groin: Involved in tinea cruris (jock itch).

  • Nail: Involved in tinea unguium (onychomycosis).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Tinea capitis → Scalp

  • Tinea corporis → Body/trunk

  • Tinea cruris → Groin

  • Tinea pedis → Foot

  • Tinea unguium → Nail

Exam Pearl:
Tinea capitis = Dermatophyte infection of the scalp.

Medicine 08.question: ৪) Which is a provocation test for potential skin allergens?
Medicine 08.exp:
Patch testing is a provocation test used to identify potential skin allergens, especially in allergic contact dermatitis. Small amounts of suspected allergens are applied to the skin (usually the back) and the reaction is assessed after a specific period.

The other options:

  • Wood's light: Uses ultraviolet light to detect certain fungal infections (e.g., some Microsporum species) and pigment disorders.

  • Magnifying glass: Used for visual examination but not an allergen provocation test.

  • Dermatoscopy: A non-invasive technique for examining skin lesions (e.g., melanoma, pigmented lesions, scabies), not for allergy testing.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Allergic contact dermatitis → Patch test

  • Immediate IgE-mediated allergy → Skin prick test

  • Fungal infection → KOH mount / Wood's lamp (selected cases)

Exam Pearl:
Patch testing is the provocation test for detecting contact skin allergens.

Medicine 08.question: ৫) Which immunoglobulin is important in defense against parasitic infection?
Medicine 08.exp:
IgE is the most important immunoglobulin involved in defense against parasitic (especially helminthic/worm) infections. IgE binds to mast cells and eosinophils, causing the release of inflammatory mediators and promoting eosinophil-mediated killing of parasites (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity).

The other options:

  • IgG: Important for systemic bacterial and viral immunity; provides opsonization and neutralization.

  • IgA: Protects mucosal surfaces (respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts).

  • IgM: First antibody produced during primary immune response.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • IgE → Parasites + Allergy

  • IgA → Mucosal immunity

  • IgG → Most abundant; secondary immune response

  • IgM → First antibody in primary response

Exam Pearl:
Helminthic parasite defense and allergic reactions → IgE.

Medicine 08.question: ৬) Which is common site for psoriasis?
Medicine 08.exp:
Psoriasis commonly affects the extensor surfaces of the body, especially:

  • Elbows

  • Knees

  • Scalp

  • Lumbosacral region

It presents as well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery-white scales due to increased epidermal turnover.

The other options:

  • Flexor surface: More commonly involved in conditions like atopic dermatitis.

  • Face: Less common site in typical psoriasis.

  • Upper trunk: Can be involved (especially guttate psoriasis), but not the classic site.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Psoriasis → Extensor surfaces

  • Classic lesions → Well-defined plaques + silvery scales

  • Auspitz sign → Pinpoint bleeding after scale removal

  • Koebner phenomenon → Lesions at sites of trauma

Exam Pearl:
Psoriasis classically affects extensor surfaces (elbows and knees).

Medicine 08.question: ৭) which is not a scabicidal drug?
Medicine 08.exp:
Tretinoin is not a scabicidal drug. It is a topical retinoid mainly used for acne vulgaris and photoaging by increasing cell turnover.

The other options are scabicidal agents used for treating scabies caused by Sarcoptes scabiei:

  • Ivermectin: Oral antiparasitic drug used especially in crusted scabies or difficult cases.

  • Permethrin: First-line topical scabicide.

  • Benzyl benzoate: Effective topical scabicide.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Scabies treatment:

    • First-line → Permethrin 5% cream

    • Alternative → Benzyl benzoate, ivermectin

  • Apply treatment to close contacts and wash clothing/bedding to prevent reinfection.

Exam Pearl:
Tretinoin is an acne drug, not a scabicide.

Medicine 08.question: ৮) Topical retinoids are used in.....?
Medicine 08.exp:
Topical retinoids (e.g., tretinoin, adapalene, tazarotene) are mainly used in the treatment of acne vulgaris. They act by:

  • Normalizing follicular keratinization

  • Preventing formation of comedones

  • Reducing microcomedones

The other options:

  • Eczema: Treated mainly with emollients and topical corticosteroids; retinoids are not routine therapy.

  • Psoriasis: Some topical retinoids (e.g., tazarotene) may be used, but they are not the primary/classic answer.

  • Scabies: Treated with scabicides like permethrin, ivermectin, and benzyl benzoate.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Topical retinoids → Acne (comedonal acne)

  • Examples: Tretinoin, Adapalene

  • Common adverse effect → Skin irritation, dryness, photosensitivity

Exam Pearl:
Topical retinoids are first-line topical agents for acne vulgaris.

Medicine 08.question: ৯) Which type of psoriasis is most common in children & adolescent?
Medicine 08.exp:
Guttate psoriasis is the most common type of psoriasis in children and adolescents. It often appears suddenly after a streptococcal throat infection and presents as multiple small, drop-like (guttate = drop) scaly lesions over the trunk and limbs.

The other options:

  • Plaque psoriasis: The most common overall type of psoriasis in all age groups, but not the typical answer for children/adolescents.

  • Pustular psoriasis: Rare; characterized by sterile pustules.

  • Erythrodermic psoriasis: Rare and severe form involving widespread redness and scaling.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Children/adolescents → Guttate psoriasis

  • Trigger → Group A Streptococcus infection

  • Most common overall → Plaque psoriasis

  • Classic lesion → Well-demarcated erythematous plaque with silvery scale

Exam Pearl:
Young patient with sudden multiple drop-like lesions after sore throat = Guttate psoriasis.

Medicine 08.question: ১০) How gonorrhoea is transmitted?
Medicine 08.exp:
Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and can be transmitted through all types of sexual contact involving infected mucosal surfaces.

Transmission can occur through:

  • Vaginal sex → common route

  • Oral sex → can cause pharyngeal gonorrhoea

  • Anal sex → can cause rectal gonorrhoea

The other options:

  • Vaginal sex: Correct but incomplete.

  • Oral sex: Correct but incomplete.

  • Anal sex: Correct but incomplete.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Organism → Neisseria gonorrhoeae

  • Transmission → Vaginal, oral, and anal sexual contact

  • Common sites:

    • Urethra

    • Cervix

    • Rectum

    • Pharynx

    • Conjunctiva

Exam Pearl:
Gonorrhoea can be transmitted by vaginal, oral, and anal sex → All of them.

Medicine 08.question: ১১) 47, XY, +18 signifies which chromosomal abnormality?
Medicine 08.exp:
47, XY, +18 indicates a male with an extra chromosome 18, i.e., trisomy 18, which is called Edward's syndrome.

The other options:

  • Down's syndrome: Caused by trisomy 21 → 47, XX/XY, +21

  • Patau's syndrome: Caused by trisomy 13 → 47, XX/XY, +13

  • Triple X syndrome: Caused by an extra X chromosome in females → 47, XXX

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Syndrome Chromosomal abnormality
Down syndrome Trisomy 21
Edward syndrome Trisomy 18
Patau syndrome Trisomy 13
Klinefelter syndrome 47, XXY
Turner syndrome 45, X

Exam Pearl:
47, XY, +18 = Edward's syndrome (Trisomy 18).

Medicine 08.question: ১২) Which is characteristic feature of gonorrhoea?
Medicine 08.exp:
The characteristic feature of gonorrhoea is mucopurulent urethral discharge due to infection of the urethral mucosa by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It is a common presentation, especially in males, often associated with dysuria.

The other options:

  • Anal discomfort: May occur in rectal gonorrhoea but is not the classic feature.

  • Rectal bleeding: Can occur in proctitis due to rectal infection, but less common.

  • Hematuria: Not a typical feature of gonorrhoea.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gonorrhoea organism → Neisseria gonorrhoeae

  • Classic presentation:

    • Mucopurulent/purulent urethral discharge

    • Dysuria

  • Complications:

    • Pelvic inflammatory disease (female)

    • Epididymo-orchitis (male)

    • Disseminated gonococcal infection

Exam Pearl:
Purulent/mucopurulent urethral discharge is the hallmark feature of gonorrhoea.

Medicine 08.question: ১৩) Commons features of Down's syndrome excludes......?
Medicine 08.exp:
Polydactyly is not a feature of Down’s syndrome. Down syndrome is caused by trisomy 21 and has characteristic physical features, intellectual disability, and congenital abnormalities.

Common features of Down syndrome include:

  • Characteristic facies (flat facial profile, epicanthic folds, upward slanting eyes)

  • Low IQ / intellectual disability

  • Congenital heart disease (especially atrioventricular septal defect)

Polydactyly (extra fingers or toes) is classically associated with Patau syndrome (trisomy 13), not Down syndrome.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Syndrome Key feature
Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) AV canal defect, intellectual disability, characteristic facies
Edward syndrome (Trisomy 18) Clenched fists, rocker-bottom feet
Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13) Polydactyly, cleft lip/palate

Exam Pearl:
Polydactyly → Patau syndrome, not Down syndrome.

Medicine 08.question: ১৪) Gram negative diplococci in microscopy is suggestive of which disease?
Medicine 08.exp:
Gram-negative diplococci seen on microscopy are characteristic of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the causative organism of gonorrhoea. In a urethral smear, they are typically seen as intracellular gram-negative diplococci within neutrophils.

The other options:

  • Syphilis: Caused by Treponema pallidum (a spirochete), not visible as gram-negative diplococci.

  • AIDS: Caused by HIV (a virus), not associated with diplococci.

  • Chancroid: Caused by Haemophilus ducreyi (gram-negative coccobacillus).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gonorrhoea → Neisseria gonorrhoeae

    • Gram-negative diplococcus

    • Kidney-bean shaped

    • Intracellular in neutrophils

  • Syphilis → Treponema pallidum

  • Chancroid → Haemophilus ducreyi

  • AIDS → HIV

Exam Pearl:
Gram-negative intracellular diplococci = Gonorrhoea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae).

Medicine 08.question: ১৫) Which is an autosomal dominant disease?
Medicine 08.exp:
Neurofibromatosis (NF type 1) is an autosomal dominant (AD) genetic disorder caused by mutation of the NF1 gene on chromosome 17. It is characterized by:

  • Café-au-lait spots

  • Neurofibromas

  • Lisch nodules

  • Increased risk of tumors

The other options:

  • Hemochromatosis: Usually autosomal recessive (HFE gene mutation).

  • Wilson's disease: Autosomal recessive (ATP7B gene mutation causing copper accumulation).

  • Sickle cell anemia: Autosomal recessive (β-globin gene mutation).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Inheritance Examples
Autosomal dominant Neurofibromatosis, Huntington disease, Marfan syndrome, AD polycystic kidney disease
Autosomal recessive Sickle cell anemia, Wilson disease, Hemochromatosis, Cystic fibrosis

Exam Pearl:
Neurofibromatosis = Autosomal dominant disease.

Medicine 08.question: ১৬) Which is conveniently recommended treatment of gonorrhoea?
Medicine 08.exp:
The recommended first-line treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhoea is a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone. Current guidelines commonly recommend ceftriaxone 500 mg IM as a single dose (dose may vary according to body weight and local guidelines).

The other options:

  • Cefixime 400 mg stat: Alternative oral therapy when ceftriaxone is not available, but less preferred due to lower effectiveness.

  • Ciprofloxacin 500 mg stat: Only used if the strain is confirmed to be ciprofloxacin-sensitive.

  • Ofloxacin 400 mg stat: Not routinely recommended because of resistance issues.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gonorrhoea organism → Neisseria gonorrhoeae

  • First-line treatment → Ceftriaxone IM stat

  • Avoid routine fluoroquinolone use due to resistance.

  • Test and treat sexual partners to prevent reinfection.

Exam Pearl:
Uncomplicated gonorrhoea → Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose.

Medicine 08.question: ১৭) Most patients with immune deficiency present with......?
Medicine 08.exp:
Most patients with immunodeficiency present with recurrent infections because the immune system is unable to effectively eliminate pathogens. The type of infection may give clues about the affected immune component:

  • B-cell defects → recurrent bacterial infections

  • T-cell defects → viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections

  • Phagocyte defects → recurrent bacterial/fungal infections

The other options:

  • Sore throat: May occur in infections but is not the typical presenting feature of immunodeficiency.

  • Skin infection: Can occur, especially in phagocyte defects, but is not the most common general presentation.

  • Septicemia: A severe complication, not the usual initial presentation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Primary immunodeficiency → recurrent, unusual, or severe infections

  • Warning signs:

    • Frequent infections

    • Poor response to antibiotics

    • Opportunistic infections

    • Family history of immunodeficiency

Exam Pearl:
Recurrent infections are the hallmark presentation of immunodeficiency.

Medicine 08.question: ১৮) Which one is common cause of non gonococcal urethritis?
Medicine 08.exp:
The most common cause of non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU) is Chlamydia trachomatis. It causes urethral inflammation without the presence of Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

The other options:

  • Treponema: Treponema pallidum causes syphilis, not NGU.

  • Mycoplasma: Mycoplasma genitalium can cause NGU, but it is less common than chlamydia.

  • Mycobacterium: Causes tuberculosis, not a typical cause of urethritis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gonococcal urethritis → Neisseria gonorrhoeae

  • Non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU) → Chlamydia trachomatis (most common)

  • Other causes of NGU:

    • Mycoplasma genitalium

    • Ureaplasma urealyticum

    • Trichomonas vaginalis

Exam Pearl:
Chlamydia trachomatis is the commonest cause of non-gonococcal urethritis.

Medicine 08.question: ১৯) Which one is autosomal recessive disorder?
Medicine 08.exp:
Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive (AR) disorder caused by mutation of the CFTR gene on chromosome 7. It leads to defective chloride transport, causing:

  • Thick mucus secretions

  • Recurrent respiratory infections

  • Pancreatic insufficiency

  • Infertility (especially in males)

The other options:

  • Huntington's disease: Autosomal dominant disorder (CAG repeat expansion in HTT gene).

  • Neurofibromatosis: Autosomal dominant disorder (NF1 gene mutation).

  • Marfan syndrome: Autosomal dominant disorder (FBN1 gene mutation).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Inheritance Examples
Autosomal recessive Cystic fibrosis, Sickle cell anemia, Wilson disease, Phenylketonuria
Autosomal dominant Huntington disease, Neurofibromatosis, Marfan syndrome

Exam Pearl:
Cystic fibrosis = Autosomal recessive disorder.

Medicine 08.question: ২০) Which is responsible for syphilis?
Medicine 08.exp:
Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum, a spirochete bacterium transmitted mainly through sexual contact. It causes a chronic infection with different stages:

  • Primary syphilis: Painless chancre

  • Secondary syphilis: Rash (including palms and soles), systemic symptoms

  • Tertiary syphilis: Neurosyphilis, cardiovascular complications

The other options:

  • Chlamydia: Causes non-gonococcal urethritis, cervicitis, and lymphogranuloma venereum.

  • Mycoplasma: Can cause non-gonococcal urethritis.

  • Gonorrhoea: Caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, not syphilis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Syphilis → Treponema pallidum

  • Type → Spirochete

  • Classic lesion → Painless genital chancre

  • Test → VDRL/RPR (screening), TPHA/FTA-ABS (confirmation)

Exam Pearl:
Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum.

Medicine 08.question: ২১) Which one is example of X-linked recessive inheritance?
Medicine 08.exp:
Hemophilia is a classic example of an X-linked recessive disorder. It is caused by mutations affecting clotting factors:

  • Hemophilia A → Factor VIII deficiency

  • Hemophilia B → Factor IX deficiency

Because males have only one X chromosome (XY), a single defective gene causes disease. Females are usually carriers because they have two X chromosomes.

The other options:

  • Sickle cell anemia: Autosomal recessive (β-globin gene mutation).

  • Cystic fibrosis: Autosomal recessive (CFTR gene mutation).

  • Neurofibromatosis: Autosomal dominant (NF1 gene mutation).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Inheritance Examples
X-linked recessive Hemophilia, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, G6PD deficiency
Autosomal recessive Sickle cell anemia, Cystic fibrosis, Wilson disease
Autosomal dominant Neurofibromatosis, Marfan syndrome, Huntington disease

Exam Pearl:
Hemophilia = X-linked recessive inheritance.

Medicine 08.question: ২২) Which is drug of choice in syphilis?
Medicine 08.exp:
The drug of choice for syphilis is penicillin, specifically benzathine penicillin G for most cases of acquired syphilis. It is highly effective against Treponema pallidum, the causative organism of syphilis.

The other options:

  • Cephalosporins: Not the first-line treatment; ceftriaxone may have activity but is not preferred.

  • Fluoroquinolones: Not recommended due to poor reliability and resistance concerns.

  • Macrolides: Azithromycin has been used in some settings but resistance limits its use.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Syphilis → Treponema pallidum

  • First-line treatment → Benzathine penicillin G

  • Neurosyphilis → Aqueous crystalline penicillin G IV

  • All stages in pregnancy → Penicillin is the only recommended therapy

Exam Pearl:
Syphilis = Benzathine penicillin G (drug of choice).

Medicine 08.question: ২৩) Stevens Johnson syndrome is a severe form of...........
Medicine 08.exp:
Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS) is considered a severe form of erythema multiforme (especially erythema multiforme major) and is a serious mucocutaneous reaction involving:

  • Skin

  • Mucous membranes (oral, ocular, genital)

It is commonly triggered by drugs (e.g., sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, NSAIDs) and infections.

The other options:

  • Erythema nodosum: A panniculitis causing tender red nodules, usually on the shins.

  • Annular erythema: Ring-shaped erythematous lesions seen in various conditions.

  • Acanthosis nigricans: Hyperpigmented, velvety thickening of skin, associated with insulin resistance.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • SJS → Severe mucocutaneous reaction

  • Major causes: Drugs and infections

  • SJS/TEN spectrum: Increasing epidermal detachment severity

    • SJS: <10% body surface area

    • TEN: >30% body surface area

Exam Pearl:
Stevens–Johnson syndrome = Severe erythema multiforme with mucosal involvement.

Medicine 08.question: ২৪) Features of Klinefelter's syndrome excludes....?
Medicine 08.exp:
Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY) is a sex chromosome disorder affecting males. It is characterized by:

  • Phenotypic male

  • Infertility due to testicular atrophy and impaired spermatogenesis

  • Gynecomastia due to increased estrogen-to-androgen ratio

  • Tall stature, small firm testes, and reduced testosterone levels

Webbed neck is not a feature of Klinefelter syndrome. It is classically associated with Turner syndrome (45, X).

The other options:

  • Phenotypic male: Correct feature of Klinefelter syndrome.

  • Infertility: Common due to azoospermia.

  • Gynecomastia: Common due to hormonal imbalance.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Syndrome Chromosome Key feature
Klinefelter 47, XXY Male, infertility, gynecomastia, small testes
Turner 45, X Female, short stature, webbed neck, coarctation of aorta

Exam Pearl:
Webbed neck → Turner syndrome, not Klinefelter syndrome.

Medicine 08.question: ২৫) Which is most common cause of genital ulceration?
Medicine 08.exp:
The most common cause of genital ulceration is genital herpes, caused by Herpes simplex virus (HSV), especially HSV-2. It typically presents with:

  • Painful grouped vesicles that rupture to form ulcers

  • Burning sensation and pain

  • Recurrent episodes due to viral latency

The other options:

  • Gonorrhoea: Causes urethral/cervical discharge and dysuria, not typically genital ulcers.

  • Syphilis: Causes a painless chancre (classic genital ulcer), but it is less common than herpes.

  • Chlamydia: Causes urethritis/cervicitis and lymphogranuloma venereum, not the commonest genital ulcer cause.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common genital ulcer disease → Genital herpes (HSV)

  • Painful ulcer → Herpes

  • Painless ulcer → Syphilis (chancre)

  • Multiple painful vesicles → HSV

  • Single painless indurated ulcer → Syphilis

Exam Pearl:
Genital ulceration most commonly occurs due to Herpes simplex virus infection.

Medicine 08.question: ২৬) Which is not a criteria of autosomal recessive diseases?
Medicine 08.option1: Half the children of unaffected carriers will be carriers
Medicine 08.option3: If both parents are carriers, 1 in 4 of children of heterozygous parents will be affected
Medicine 08.option4: Usually only one generation is affected
Medicine 08.exp:
Autosomal recessive (AR) diseases affect both males and females equally because the defective gene is located on an autosome (non-sex chromosome). Therefore, the statement “It affects only male” is not a criterion of autosomal recessive inheritance.

The other options:

  • Half the children of unaffected carriers will be carriers: Correct. If one parent is a carrier (Aa) and the other is unaffected (AA), 50% of children may be carriers.

  • If both parents are carriers, 1 in 4 children will be affected: Correct (Aa × Aa → 25% AA, 50% Aa, 25% aa).

  • Usually only one generation is affected: Correct; AR diseases often appear among siblings but may skip generations.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Autosomal recessive:

    • Both sexes affected equally

    • Parents usually unaffected carriers

    • 25% affected, 50% carriers, 25% normal (carrier × carrier)

    • Often seen in a single generation

Exam Pearl:
AR disorders do not show male-only inheritance; sex distribution is equal.

Medicine 08.question: ২৭) Which immunoglobulin is highly effective in agglutinating pathogens?
Medicine 08.exp:
IgM is the most effective immunoglobulin for agglutination of pathogens because it is a pentamer with 10 antigen-binding sites, allowing it to bind multiple antigens simultaneously and produce strong agglutination.

The other options:

  • IgG: Important for opsonization, neutralization, and complement activation; it is the major antibody in secondary immune responses.

  • IgA: Provides mucosal immunity in secretions (saliva, tears, breast milk).

  • IgE: Involved in allergic reactions and defense against helminths.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • IgM → Best agglutinating antibody; first antibody produced

  • IgG → Most abundant immunoglobulin; crosses placenta

  • IgA → Mucosal protection

  • IgE → Allergy + parasites

Exam Pearl:
IgM, due to its pentameric structure, is the most powerful agglutinating immunoglobulin.

Medicine 08.question: ২৮) Which drug causes hair loss?
Medicine 08.exp:
Isotretinoin (an oral retinoid used mainly for severe acne) can cause hair loss (alopecia) as a side effect. The hair loss is usually temporary and reversible after discontinuation.

The other options:

  • Minoxidil: A drug used to promote hair growth in androgenetic alopecia.

  • Oral retinoids: This group can cause hair thinning, but isotretinoin is the commonly tested example.

  • Benzoyl peroxide: A topical acne medication; may cause irritation but not typically hair loss.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Isotretinoin adverse effects:

    • Dry lips (cheilitis) — most common

    • Dry skin

    • Teratogenicity

    • Raised liver enzymes/lipids

    • Alopecia (hair loss)

Exam Pearl:
Isotretinoin → Acne treatment drug associated with reversible hair loss.

Medicine 08.question: ২৯) Which one is primary lesion of syphilis?
Medicine 08.exp:
The primary lesion of syphilis is a chancre. It appears at the site of Treponema pallidum inoculation, usually 2–3 weeks after infection. A typical chancre is:

  • Painless

  • Clean-based

  • Indurated ulcer

  • Associated with regional lymphadenopathy

The other options:

  • Chancroid: Caused by Haemophilus ducreyi; produces a painful genital ulcer.

  • Maculopapular lesion: Seen in secondary syphilis (especially rash involving palms and soles).

  • Condylomata lata: Also a feature of secondary syphilis; broad moist papules.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Primary syphilis → Chancre (painless ulcer)

  • Secondary syphilis → Maculopapular rash + condylomata lata

  • Tertiary syphilis → Gummas, cardiovascular and neurological complications

Exam Pearl:
Syphilis primary lesion = painless chancre.

Medicine 08.question: ৩০) Features of Turner's syndrome excludes.....?
Medicine 08.exp:
Turner syndrome (45, X) is a chromosomal disorder affecting females. The typical features include:

  • Phenotypic female

  • Webbed neck

  • Primary amenorrhoea due to gonadal dysgenesis (streak ovaries)

Tall stature is not a feature of Turner syndrome; instead, patients usually have short stature.

The other options:

  • Phenotypic female: Correct feature.

  • Webbed neck: Classic feature due to lymphatic developmental abnormality.

  • Primary amenorrhoea: Common due to ovarian failure.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Syndrome Chromosome Key features
Turner syndrome 45, X Female, short stature, webbed neck, primary amenorrhoea
Klinefelter syndrome 47, XXY Male, tall stature, infertility, gynecomastia

Exam Pearl:
Turner syndrome = Short female with webbed neck and primary amenorrhoea.

Medicine 08.question: ৩১) Features of syphilitic lymph node excludes......?
Medicine 08.exp:
In syphilis, especially primary and secondary syphilis, lymphadenopathy is typically:

  • Discrete

  • Rubbery

  • Non-tender

  • Mobile (not fixed)

Therefore, fixed lymph nodes are not a feature of syphilitic lymphadenopathy.

The other options:

  • Discrete: Correct; nodes are usually separate rather than matted.

  • Rubbery: Correct classic description.

  • Non-tender: Correct; syphilitic lymph nodes are usually painless.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Syphilitic lymphadenopathy:

    • Generalized (especially secondary syphilis)

    • Rubbery

    • Discrete

    • Non-tender

    • Mobile

Exam Pearl:
Syphilis lymph nodes are rubbery, discrete, non-tender, and mobile — not fixed.

Medicine 08.question: ৩২) Which is not a physiological cause of secondary immune deficiency?
Medicine 08.exp:
Secondary immune deficiency can occur due to physiological states that temporarily reduce immune function, such as:

  • Ageing → immunosenescence (reduced immune response)

  • Pregnancy → altered immunity to tolerate the fetus

  • Prematurity → immature immune system

Growing age is not considered a physiological cause of secondary immune deficiency. Normal growth is not associated with immune suppression.

The other options:

  • Ageing: Correct physiological cause.

  • Pregnancy: Correct physiological cause.

  • Prematurity: Correct due to immature immune defenses.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Physiological secondary immune deficiency:

    • Ageing

    • Pregnancy

    • Prematurity

  • Common pathological causes:

    • HIV infection

    • Malignancy

    • Immunosuppressive drugs

    • Malnutrition

Exam Pearl:
Normal growing age is not a cause of secondary immunodeficiency.

Medicine 08.question: ৩৩) Which is not a criteria of autosomal dominant diseases?
Medicine 08.option2: Half of the offsprings are affected
Medicine 08.option3: Both male and female are equally affected
Medicine 08.option4: Unaffected individual can transmit the disease
Medicine 08.exp:
In autosomal dominant (AD) diseases, an affected individual usually has one mutant allele and can transmit the disease to offspring. Unaffected individuals generally do not transmit the disease (except in rare cases like incomplete penetrance or new mutations).

The other options:

  • Consecutive generations are affected: Correct — AD disorders often show vertical transmission.

  • Half of the offspring are affected: Correct — an affected heterozygous parent (Aa) has a 50% chance of passing the disease.

  • Both male and female are equally affected: Correct — the gene is on an autosome, not a sex chromosome.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Autosomal dominant:

    • Affects males and females equally

    • Appears in every generation

    • Affected heterozygous parent → 50% affected children

    • Examples: Marfan syndrome, Huntington disease, Neurofibromatosis

Exam Pearl:
In autosomal dominant inheritance, unaffected individuals usually do not transmit the disease.

Medicine 08.question: ৩৪) Which is the key feature of cardiovascular syphilis?
Medicine 08.exp:
The key feature of cardiovascular syphilis is syphilitic aortitis. It occurs mainly in tertiary syphilis due to chronic infection by Treponema pallidum, affecting the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta. This can lead to:

  • Aortic root dilatation

  • Aortic regurgitation

  • Formation of aortic aneurysm

The other options:

  • Endocarditis: Not the characteristic cardiovascular manifestation of syphilis.

  • Myocarditis: Not the main feature.

  • Pericarditis: Not typical of cardiovascular syphilis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Tertiary syphilis complications:

    • Cardiovascular syphilis → Aortitis

    • Neurosyphilis → Tabes dorsalis, general paresis

    • Gummatous lesions

  • Syphilitic aortitis mainly affects the ascending aorta.

Exam Pearl:
Cardiovascular syphilis = Syphilitic aortitis (ascending aorta involvement).

Medicine 08.question: ৩৫) Which is X-linked dominant diseases?
Medicine 08.exp:
Vitamin-D resistant rickets (X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets) is a classic example of an X-linked dominant (XLD) disorder. It is caused by mutation of the PHEX gene on the X chromosome, leading to renal phosphate wasting and defective bone mineralization.

The other options:

  • Huntington's disease: Autosomal dominant (HTT gene mutation).

  • Neurofibromatosis: Autosomal dominant (NF1 gene mutation).

  • Marfan syndrome: Autosomal dominant (FBN1 gene mutation).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Inheritance Examples
X-linked dominant Vitamin-D resistant rickets, Rett syndrome, Fragile X syndrome
X-linked recessive Hemophilia, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, G6PD deficiency
Autosomal dominant Huntington disease, Marfan syndrome, Neurofibromatosis

Exam Pearl:
Vitamin-D resistant rickets = X-linked dominant disorder.

Medicine 08.question: ৩৬) Which immunoglobulin is highly effective at neutralising toxins?
Medicine 08.exp:
IgG is highly effective in neutralising toxins and viruses by binding to them and preventing their interaction with host cells. It is the major immunoglobulin involved in secondary immune responses and provides long-term protection.

The other options:

  • IgA: Mainly provides mucosal immunity in secretions such as saliva, tears, and breast milk.

  • IgM: Best for agglutination and is the first antibody produced in primary immune response.

  • IgE: Involved in allergic reactions and defense against helminths.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • IgG → Neutralization, opsonization, crosses placenta

  • IgM → Agglutination, first antibody produced

  • IgA → Mucosal protection

  • IgE → Allergy + parasites

Exam Pearl:
IgG is the main immunoglobulin responsible for toxin neutralization.

Medicine 08.question: ৩৭) Which is a non specific test for syphilis?
Medicine 08.exp:
VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test) is a non-specific (non-treponemal) test for syphilis. It detects reagin antibodies against cardiolipin antigen rather than antibodies specifically against Treponema pallidum.

The other options are specific (treponemal) tests:

  • TPHA (Treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay): Detects antibodies specific to T. pallidum.

  • FTA-ABS (Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test): Highly specific treponemal test.

  • EIA (Enzyme immunoassay): Detects treponemal antibodies.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Type Tests
Non-treponemal (non-specific) VDRL, RPR
Treponemal (specific) TPHA, FTA-ABS, EIA

Exam Pearl:
VDRL/RPR = non-specific screening tests for syphilis.

Medicine 08.question: ৩৮) Hutchinson’s teeth is a stigmata of which disease?
Medicine 08.exp:
Hutchinson’s teeth are a classic stigmata of congenital syphilis caused by infection with Treponema pallidum during pregnancy. They are characterized by:

  • Notched, screw-driver shaped upper central incisors

  • Abnormal development of permanent teeth

Other classic features of congenital syphilis include Hutchinson’s triad:

  1. Hutchinson teeth

  2. Interstitial keratitis

  3. Sensorineural deafness

The other options:

  • Gonorrhoea: Caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae; not associated with Hutchinson teeth.

  • AIDS: Caused by HIV; no such dental stigma.

  • Herpes: Causes vesicular lesions, not Hutchinson teeth.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Congenital syphilis → Hutchinson triad

    • Hutchinson teeth

    • Interstitial keratitis

    • 8th nerve deafness

Exam Pearl:
Hutchinson’s teeth = Congenital syphilis.

Medicine 08.question: ৩৯) 47, XY, +13 signifies which chromosomal abnormality?
Medicine 08.exp:
47, XY, +13 indicates a male with an extra chromosome 13, i.e., trisomy 13, which is called Patau syndrome.

The other options:

  • Down's syndrome: Caused by trisomy 21 → 47, XX/XY, +21

  • Edward's syndrome: Caused by trisomy 18 → 47, XX/XY, +18

  • Triple X syndrome: Caused by an extra X chromosome in females → 47, XXX

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Syndrome Chromosomal abnormality Key features
Patau syndrome Trisomy 13 Cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, severe defects
Edward syndrome Trisomy 18 Clenched fists, rocker-bottom feet
Down syndrome Trisomy 21 Intellectual disability, characteristic facies

Exam Pearl:
47, XY, +13 = Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13).

Medicine 08.question: ৪০) Which one is indicated in syphilis patient allergic to penicillin?
Medicine 08.exp:
In a syphilis patient allergic to penicillin (except pregnancy and neurosyphilis situations where penicillin is mandatory), doxycycline is an accepted alternative treatment. It is effective against Treponema pallidum.

The other options:

  • Tetracycline: Also effective, but doxycycline is more commonly preferred due to better tolerability and dosing convenience.

  • Azithromycin: Not recommended routinely because of increasing macrolide resistance in T. pallidum.

  • Ciprofloxacin: Not effective and not recommended for syphilis treatment.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Syphilis first-line → Benzathine penicillin G

  • Penicillin allergy (non-pregnant) → Doxycycline

  • Pregnancy + penicillin allergy → Penicillin desensitization and treatment

  • Neurosyphilis → IV aqueous crystalline penicillin G

Exam Pearl:
Penicillin-allergic syphilis patient → Doxycycline is the preferred alternative.

Medicine 08.question: ৪১) Dithranol & coal tar are mainly used in......?
Medicine 08.exp:
Dithranol (anthralin) and coal tar are traditional topical treatments mainly used for psoriasis. They work by reducing excessive epidermal cell proliferation and inflammation.

The other options:

  • Acne: Treated with topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, antibiotics, etc.

  • Eczema: Mainly treated with emollients and topical corticosteroids.

  • Scabies: Treated with scabicides like permethrin and ivermectin.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Psoriasis topical treatments:

    • Dithranol (anthralin)

    • Coal tar

    • Topical corticosteroids

    • Vitamin D analogues (calcipotriol)

    • Retinoids (tazarotene)

Exam Pearl:
Dithranol + coal tar = classic topical therapy for psoriasis.

Medicine 08.question: ৪২) Which is a pathognomonic lesion of acne ?
Medicine 08.exp:
The pathognomonic lesion of acne vulgaris is the comedone. It occurs due to follicular plugging with sebum and keratin.

Types of comedones:

  • Open comedone (blackhead) → oxidized keratin/sebum

  • Closed comedone (whitehead) → blocked follicle beneath the skin

The other options:

  • Papule: Can occur in inflammatory acne but is not pathognomonic.

  • Crust: Seen in healing lesions or secondary infection, not typical of acne.

  • Burrow: Pathognomonic of scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Acne → Comedones

  • Scabies → Burrows

  • Psoriasis → Silvery plaques

  • Gonorrhoea → Mucopurulent discharge

Exam Pearl:
Comedone is the hallmark/pathognomonic lesion of acne vulgaris.

Medicine 08.question: ৪৩) Which type of tinea occurs in sole & palm?
Medicine 08.exp:
Tinea manuum is a dermatophyte fungal infection involving the hands, particularly the palms. It causes:

  • Dry scaling

  • Hyperkeratosis

  • Itching of the palm

The sole of the foot is usually affected by tinea pedis, but among the given options, tinea manuum is the closest and correct answer for palm involvement.

The other options:

  • Tinea capitis: Infection of the scalp and hair.

  • Tinea unguium: Infection of the nails (onychomycosis).

  • Tinea cruris: Infection of the groin.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Tinea capitis → Scalp

  • Tinea manuum → Hand/palm

  • Tinea pedis → Foot/sole

  • Tinea cruris → Groin

  • Tinea unguium → Nail

Exam Pearl:
Palm involvement = Tinea manuum (sole involvement is classically tinea pedis).

Medicine 08.question: ৪৪) Which has revolutionised the treatment of moderate to severe acne?
Medicine 08.exp:
Isotretinoin has revolutionised the treatment of moderate to severe acne, especially severe nodulocystic acne and acne resistant to conventional therapy. It is an oral retinoid that acts on all major pathogenic factors of acne by:

  • Markedly reducing sebaceous gland activity

  • Decreasing sebum production

  • Normalizing follicular keratinization

  • Reducing Cutibacterium acnes colonization

  • Reducing inflammation

The other options:

  • Benzoyl peroxide: Effective topical antibacterial agent, mainly for mild to moderate acne.

  • Retinoids: Important topical therapy, especially comedonal acne, but not the revolutionary systemic treatment.

  • OCP: Useful in selected females with hormonal acne, but not for severe acne generally.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Severe acne → Oral isotretinoin

  • Major adverse effects:

    • Teratogenicity

    • Cheilitis

    • Dry skin

    • Raised lipids/LFTs

    • Mood changes (rare)

Exam Pearl:
Isotretinoin is the drug that transformed the management of moderate to severe acne.

Medicine 08.question: ৪৫) Which type of topical corticosteroids are preferred for chronic eczema?
Medicine 08.exp:
Ointment preparations of topical corticosteroids are preferred for chronic eczema because they are:

  • More occlusive

  • Better at increasing penetration of the steroid into thick, dry, lichenified skin

  • More moisturizing than creams or lotions

The other options:

  • Cream: Less greasy and suitable for acute, weeping eczema.

  • Lotion: Useful for hairy areas or large surface areas but less effective for chronic dry eczema.

  • Gel: Less commonly used and may cause irritation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ointment → Chronic, dry, lichenified eczema

  • Cream → Acute/subacute eczema

  • Lotion → Scalp/hairy areas

  • Potency should be selected according to site and severity.

Exam Pearl:
Chronic eczema with dry thick skin → Use topical corticosteroid ointment.

Medicine 08.question: ৪৬) Which is the most common presentation of psoriasis?
Medicine 08.exp:
Plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris) is the most common presentation of psoriasis, accounting for the majority of cases. It presents with:

  • Well-demarcated, erythematous plaques

  • Covered by silvery-white scales

  • Commonly affecting extensor surfaces (elbows and knees), scalp, and lumbosacral region

The other options:

  • Guttate psoriasis: Common in children and young adults, often following streptococcal infection, but not the most common overall.

  • Pustular psoriasis: Rare, characterized by sterile pustules.

  • Erythrodermic psoriasis: Rare and severe form involving widespread erythema and scaling.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common psoriasis type → Plaque psoriasis

  • Children/adolescents → Guttate psoriasis

  • Severe generalized form → Erythrodermic psoriasis

  • Pustules → Pustular psoriasis

Exam Pearl:
Psoriasis most commonly presents as plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris).

Medicine 08.question: ৪৭) What is expected finding in CBC of urticaria patient?
Medicine 08.exp:
In urticaria (hives), the expected CBC finding may be eosinophilia, especially when the condition is related to allergic reactions or parasitic infestation. Eosinophils are associated with IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reactions.

The other options:

  • Neutrophilia: Suggests bacterial infection or acute inflammation, not typical of urticaria.

  • Lymphocytosis: Seen in some viral infections, not a characteristic finding.

  • Monocytosis: Associated with chronic infections or inflammatory conditions, not typical.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Urticaria → Type I hypersensitivity reaction

  • Mediator → Histamine release from mast cells

  • Immunoglobulin involved → IgE

  • CBC may show → Eosinophilia (especially allergic/parasitic causes)

Exam Pearl:
Urticaria is commonly associated with eosinophilia due to allergic hypersensitivity.

Medicine 08.question: ৪৮) Which is most common immunobullous disease?
Medicine 08.exp:
Bullous pemphigoid is the most common immunobullous disease. It is an autoimmune subepidermal blistering disorder caused by antibodies against:

  • BP180 (type XVII collagen)

  • BP230
    located in the basement membrane zone.

It typically affects elderly patients and presents with:

  • Tense, itchy blisters

  • Urticarial or erythematous plaques

  • Usually no mucosal involvement

The other options:

  • Pemphigus vulgaris: Common autoimmune blistering disease but less common than bullous pemphigoid; causes flaccid intraepidermal blisters.

  • Dermatitis herpetiformis: Associated with coeliac disease; causes grouped itchy vesicles.

  • Pemphigoid gestationis: Rare autoimmune blistering disease occurring during pregnancy.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Disease Level of blister Antibody
Bullous pemphigoid Subepidermal BP180/BP230
Pemphigus vulgaris Intraepidermal Desmoglein 3
Dermatitis herpetiformis Subepidermal IgA deposits

Exam Pearl:
Most common immunobullous disease = Bullous pemphigoid.

Medicine 08.question: ৪৯) Development of patches of hypopigmentation due to focal loss of memelanocyte is known as....?
Medicine 08.exp:
Vitiligo is an acquired depigmentation disorder caused by focal loss/destruction of melanocytes, leading to well-defined hypopigmented or depigmented patches on the skin.

The other options:

  • Albinism: A congenital disorder due to reduced or absent melanin production caused by genetic defects; melanocytes are present but melanin synthesis is impaired.

  • Pityriasis alba: Causes mild hypopigmented patches, usually in children, due to dermatitis-related changes, not melanocyte loss.

  • Pityriasis versicolor: A fungal infection caused by Malassezia species causing hypo/hyperpigmented scaly patches.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Vitiligo → Loss of melanocytes

  • Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes

  • Common sites: face, hands, genital areas, pressure points

  • Associated with autoimmune diseases (e.g., thyroid disease)

Exam Pearl:
Focal loss of melanocytes causing depigmented patches = Vitiligo.

Medicine 08.question: ৫০) Ophthalmia neonatorum is caused by....?
Medicine 08.exp:
Ophthalmia neonatorum (neonatal conjunctivitis) is classically caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae acquired during passage through an infected birth canal. It usually presents within the first 2–5 days of life with:

  • Severe purulent conjunctival discharge

  • Eyelid swelling

  • Risk of corneal ulceration and blindness

The other options:

  • T. pallidum (Treponema pallidum): Causes congenital syphilis, not typical ophthalmia neonatorum.

  • H. ducreyi: Causes chancroid.

  • CMV: Causes congenital infection (e.g., hearing loss, neurological abnormalities), not the common cause of neonatal conjunctivitis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common cause of ophthalmia neonatorum (classically tested) → N. gonorrhoeae

  • Chlamydia trachomatis is also a common cause and often presents later (5–14 days).

  • Prevention → Erythromycin eye ointment (varies by guideline).

Exam Pearl:
Ophthalmia neonatorum with severe purulent discharge → Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
